tt_um_Electom_cla_4bits.how: A 4-bit adder built the fast way. Instead of letting each carry ripple from one bit to the next, like adding by hand, it works out for every bit whether that position makes a carry (a AND b) or passes one along (a OR b), then computes all four carries at once from those signals. The 4-bit sum s and the carry out co are saved in flip-flops on each clock edge, so the answer appears after Step. Decap's decompiler recognises the whole circuit as a single a + b + ci.
tt_um_Electom_cla_4bits.try: Set a to 9, b to 8 and ci to 0, then press Step: s shows 1 and co shows 1, because 9 + 8 = 17 is 10001 in binary.

tt_um_JAC_EE_segdecode.how: This chip drives four 7-segment displays and scans a keypad on behalf of a microcontroller that talks to it over SPI. While EN is 1, each clock pushes the MOSI bit into an 8-bit shift register, like appending bits to a queue. When EN falls, the byte is copied into an output register: the low 4 bits go through hand-simplified logic that lights the digit 0 to 9, the next 2 bits pick which display is active (one ScreenSel line pulled to 0), and the top 2 bits pick one of the four KeyPlxr keypad lines to send back, inverted, on MISO. Segments are active low (0 means lit) and all switch off while EN is 0.
tt_um_JAC_EE_segdecode.try: Set EN to 1 and MOSI to 1, press Step 3 times, then set EN to 0 and back to 1: the byte 7 is latched, so Out7S reads 15 (segments A, B and C lit, the digit 7) and ScreenSel reads 14 (display 0 selected).

tt_um_Richard28277.how: A tiny calculator: two 4-bit numbers and a 4-bit opcode go in, and on each clock edge the chosen answer is saved into an 8-bit result register. Inside, every operation is computed at the same time (add, subtract, multiply, divide, AND, OR, XOR, NOT, and an XOR with the fixed key 0xAB that the authors call encryption), and a big multiplexer, like a switch statement, keeps the one the opcode names. Add and subtract also set the carry_out and overflow flags, and opcodes 9 to 15 give 0. The author's code reads its first operand from the upper input pins, so the simulator's a and b are swapped for subtract, divide and NOT.
tt_um_Richard28277.try: Set a to 6, b to 7 and opcode to 2 (multiply), then press Step: result shows 42.

tt_um_brailliance.how: The team wrote an ASCII to Braille converter: a lookup table from characters to 6-dot patterns, a small memory holding the text, and a state machine that hands out one Braille cell each time next is pressed. But the top-level file that was manufactured never connects any of it. It still holds the Tiny Tapeout template line uo_out = ui_in + uio_in, so the silicon is just an 8-bit adder of the two input buses and the synthesis tool dropped the unused Braille logic. Decap's decompiled source shows exactly that one addition.
tt_um_brailliance.try: Set next to 1 and reader1_out shows 4 at once, then set reset to 1 as well and it shows 6, because the pins named clk, reset and next simply pass through the adder as the values 1, 2 and 4.

tt_um_clock_divider_arghunter.how: Despite the microphone pin names, the manufactured chip is only a clock divider. It counts rising edges of a clock fed in on pin ui_in[0] and flips its output each time the count reaches a ratio set on ui_in[1] to ui_in[7], like a loop that toggles a flag every N ticks. A nonzero delay value on the bidirectional pins (labelled Delay_Select, Beamformed_PCM_Output and Mic_Clock here) holds the count to shift the output's timing, which the author calls lag correction. The labels come from a larger microphone beamforming design whose files sit in the same repo but were not built, so only PCM_Out_Mic_0 is driven (it is the divided clock) and the other outputs are always 0.
tt_um_clock_divider_arghunter.try: There is no live behaviour to see, because Step and Run drive the main clk while this chip only counts edges on ui_in[0], which is not among the inputs shown, so PCM_Out_Mic_0 stays at 0 and the most useful thing is to click its flip-flops in the layout to find the counter.

tt_um_dpmu.how: A dynamic power manager: the controller that decides how fast, and at what voltage, a processor's two cores and its memory should run. Inside is a 5-state state machine (normal, performance, power save, thermal management, battery saving) that reads a performance request, temperature, battery level and workload, and each state drives fixed voltage and frequency codes onto uo_out and uio_out. The mode register updates on the rising clock edge and the outputs and next mode are worked out on the falling edge, so the codes are only levels for external regulators to act on. The published pinout gives no usable input names, so in the simulator every input reads 0, which looks like an empty battery.
tt_um_dpmu.try: Press Reset and uo_out shows 73 and uio_out shows 42 (normal mode, medium voltage and frequency), then press Step and they drop to 0 and 1, because with the battery reading empty it moves to battery saving with everything at minimum and power_save on.

tt_um_dpmunit.how: The same dynamic power manager as DPMU, submitted a second time by the same team with identical code. A 5-state state machine (normal, performance, power save, thermal management, battery saving) reads a performance request, temperature, battery level and workload, and each state drives fixed voltage and frequency codes for two cores and memory onto uo_out and uio_out. The mode register updates on the rising clock edge and the outputs and next mode are worked out on the falling edge. The published pinout gives no usable input names, so in the simulator every input reads 0, which looks like an empty battery.
tt_um_dpmunit.try: Press Reset and uo_out shows 73 and uio_out shows 42 (normal mode), then press Step and they drop to 0 and 1, because with the battery reading empty it moves to battery saving with everything at minimum and power_save on.

tt_um_emmyxu_obstacle_detection.how: Pure combinational logic with no clock or memory, like a small if/else function. It reads two obstacle sensors and picks a buzzer: if only the left sensor sees something it buzzes the right side, if only the right sensor does it buzzes the left side, and if both do it sends a separate both close code to each side. Each buzzer actually gets a 2-bit code on output pins 0 to 3, but the author's pinout only names pins 0 and 1, so the simulator shows part of the picture. The pin labelled reset is not wired, the chip's real reset is rst_n.
tt_um_emmyxu_obstacle_detection.try: Set sensor_left and sensor_right to 1 and left_buzz shows 1 straight away (the both close code), then set sensor_left back to 0 and right_buzz shows 1, because pin 1 really carries the left buzzer's close bit.

tt_um_factory_test.how: This is the test design Tiny Tapeout uses to check that the silicon works. Inside is an 8-bit counter that adds 1 on every clock, plus multiplexers (switches that pick one of several inputs). Pin ui_in[0] chooses what the outputs show: the counter when it is 1, a copy of the uio_in pins when it is 0, and while reset is held low the outputs echo ui_in straight back.
tt_um_factory_test.try: There is no output readout here because the select pin ui_in[0] has no input box and reads 0, so press Run and watch the counter's flip-flops flip in the 3D view while the outputs quietly copy uio_in.

tt_um_fountaincoder_top_ad.how: The author calls it a temporal add. Every clock, a 4-bit accumulator adds in[0] to in[3] to a running total that wraps past 15, and the upper four input bits are unused. A flag switches on when the total reaches 1 and off once it reaches 4, and on every clock the flag is on a second counter steps forward (the author's file is named gray_count.v). The 8 out bits are a registered copy of that counter, shown only on clocks where the total is 4 or more.
tt_um_fountaincoder_top_ad.try: Expect out to stay at 0 whatever you type in in, because this chip treats rst_n as active high and only runs while reset is held low, and the Reset button holds it low for just one clock.

tt_um_i2c_peripheral_stevej.how: An I2C peripheral is a device that listens on a two-wire bus, where SCL is the clock and a data line carries the bits. This chip uses SCL itself as its clock: a shift register collects 8 bits (a 7-bit address plus a read flag) and a small state machine then decides the reply. Address 0x2A answers with the byte 0x55, address 0x55 answers with 0xAA, and any other address gets 0xCC. The code reads incoming data from pin uio_in[6], not from the SDA pin, and it also keeps the template line that adds ui_in and uio_in onto uo_out.
tt_um_i2c_peripheral_stevej.try: Step does nothing and toggling SCL between 1 and 0 changes nothing either, because the chip's own reset pin uio_in[1] has no input box and reads 0, which holds every flip-flop in reset.

tt_um_i2s_to_pwm_arghunter.how: It turns a digital audio stream (I2S) into pulses that can drive a speaker. On each tick of the bit clock on ui_in[0], a 16-bit shift register takes in one bit from ui_in[2], and when the left/right clock on ui_in[1] flips, the top 8 bits are saved as the left or right sample. Two PWM generators compare each sample with a counter that runs 0 to 191, so each output stays high for a share of time that matches the sample, like a dimmer switch. The pin labels come from a different project: only PCM_Out_Mic_0 (left) and PCM_Out_Mic_1 (right) are driven, and the rest are tied to 0.
tt_um_i2s_to_pwm_arghunter.try: Nothing moves here because the chip runs on the I2S bit clock at ui_in[0], which has no input box, so Step and Run leave every output at 0.

tt_um_kapilan_alarm.how: A 24-hour clock where each clock cycle counts as one second. Three chained counters work like an odometer: seconds go 0 to 59, each wrap bumps minutes 0 to 59, and each minutes wrap bumps hours 0 to 23. A comparator checks the time against alarm_hours and alarm_minutes on every tick, and a match sets an alarm flag (pin uio_out[7], not shown in the readout) that also freezes the clock. With the alarm left at 0:00 it matches straight away, so set an alarm before you run it.
tt_um_kapilan_alarm.try: Set alarm_minutes to 2, press Reset, then Run: minutes goes up by 1 every 60 clocks and freezes at 2 when the alarm fires, while hours stays 0.

tt_um_kb2ghz_xalu.how: A 4-bit ALU, the part of a CPU that does the maths, built only from logic gates with no clock or memory. A ripple-carry adder and a set of bitwise gates all compute at once, and the function code F2 F1 F0 picks one result: 0 add, 1 AND, 2 OR, 3 XOR, 4 pass A, 5 pass B, 6 shift right, 7 shift left. COM flips every result bit (ones' complement), ci_right and ci_left are the carry or shift inputs, and comparators raise EQU when A equals B, ZERO when the result is 0 and NEG_ZERO when it is all ones.
tt_um_kb2ghz_xalu.try: Set da0, da1, db0 and db2 to 1 (A is 3, B is 5) with F0, F1 and F2 at 0 and only d3 lights (3 plus 5 is 8) the moment you type, then set F0 to 1 for AND and only d0 stays lit (3 AND 5 is 1).

tt_um_mac.how: A multiply-accumulate unit, the core step of neural-network chips: it multiplies A (ui_in[0] to ui_in[3]) by B (uio_in) and adds the product to a running total shown on uo_out. It is a pipeline of registers: a Dadda multiplier (a fast tree of adders) feeds a product register, a Kogge-Stone adder adds that to the total, and the sum feeds back, so the total grows by A times B every two clocks. As built, the multiplier gives wrong answers for many inputs, for example 3 times 3 comes out as 7.
tt_um_mac.try: Only B has an input box here (uio_in) and A reads as 0, so every product is 0 and uo_out stays at 0 however many times you Step.

tt_um_ring_divider.how: A ring oscillator is a loop of inverting gates that keeps chasing its own output, flipping as fast as the gates can switch. The author wrote five NAND gates, but synthesis collapsed them into a single gate that feeds back on itself, enabled when tst_clk and ena are both 1. Its output drives seven flip-flops chained as a ripple divider, each halving the frequency, so final_out runs 128 times slower than osc_out. The other outputs just echo ring taps (n1, n3, n2_buf, n4_buf) and the ena, clk and rst_n pins.
tt_um_ring_divider.try: Set tst_clk to 1 and osc_out jumps to 1 and stays there, because this simulator has no gate delays, so the real oscillation and the divided final_out cannot appear.

tt_um_sign_addsub.how: A 4-bit calculator that can add or subtract two signed numbers a and b. Each sign bit picks whether its operand is negated: the chip flips every bit of that operand with XOR gates, then feeds the sign bit in as an extra carry, which is the flip-the-bits-and-add-one trick for two's complement. A row of half adders and full adders then adds the two values with no clock and no memory. The answer s is 4 bits and wraps around, so 13 on the outputs means minus 3.
tt_um_sign_addsub.try: Set a0 and a2 to 1 (a is 5), b1 to 1 (b is 2) and sign0 to 1: s0 and s1 light at once, which is 3 because the chip worked out 5 minus 2.

tt_um_wokwi_407306064811090945.how: A silicon experiment, not a function. Five flip-flops sample input pins: one is a normal flop that captures on the rising clock edge. The other four are clocked by a pulse generator that XORs the clock with a copy of itself delayed through a chain of inverters (the pin names say 1, 3, 5 and 7 inverters), so they get a short pulse on every rising and falling edge and capture twice per cycle. The aim is to measure on the real chip how narrow a clock pulse a flop still obeys, which depends on gate delay that the zero-delay simulator cannot show, so here those pulses never happen.
tt_um_wokwi_407306064811090945.try: There are no inputs on the simulator bar, so Step only shows q_for_normal_flop staying 0 and clk back at 0 after each cycle. Click the cells near the clock pin instead to follow the inverter chains that build each pulse.

tt_um_wokwi_407760296956596225.how: A pocket calculator for two 3-bit numbers (0 to 7) with a 2-bit operation code. Both operation bits at 0 adds the numbers and wraps past 7, lighting the decimal point when it overflows. Operation_bit_1 alone gives bitwise AND, Operation_bit_2 alone gives OR and both give XOR. The result goes straight through a lookup table that turns the digit into which of the seven display segments light, all as one block of gates with no clock.
tt_um_wokwi_407760296956596225.try: Set Operand_A_bit_2 and Operand_B_bit_2 to 1 with both operation bits at 0: Segment_B, Segment_C, Segment_F and Segment_G light at once to draw a 4, because 2 plus 2 is 4 (only the middle bit of each operand is on the bar, the other bits stay 0).

tt_um_wokwi_407852791999030273.how: A tiny bus-based computer datapath, like a breadboard CPU. An 8-bit shift register takes one bit from SI on every clock, and two 8-bit registers A and B load whatever is on the shared bus when LA or LB is 1 at a clock. Enable lines choose who drives the bus: ESO puts the shift register there, DIRA and DIRB put A or B there, and EAO puts the adder's result A plus B there (A minus B when AS is 1). OUT0 to OUT7 always show the bus.
tt_um_wokwi_407852791999030273.try: Set SI to 1 and press Step three times, then set SI to 0 and ESO to 1: OUT0, OUT1 and OUT2 light because the shift register now holds 7 (set LA to 1 and Step once more to copy that 7 into register A).

tt_um_wokwi_408118380088342529.how: Despite the name, there is no timer or memory inside. It is a small decoder that turns a 2-bit code into one of three lights: Out_1 is on when Input_1 is 0, Out_3 is on when Input_1 is 1 and Input_2 is 0, and Out_2 simply copies Input_2. The actual sequence has to come from whoever flips the two switches.
tt_um_wokwi_408118380088342529.try: Outputs update immediately: with both inputs at 0 only Out_1 is on, set Input_1 to 1 and only Out_3 is on, then set Input_2 to 1 as well and only Out_2 is on.

tt_um_wokwi_408216451206371329.how: Two checks on all eight inputs at once, with no clock. Out_0 is a parity bit: an XOR of all eight inputs, so it is 1 when an odd number of switches are on. Out_1 is an 8-input AND, so it is 1 only when every switch is on. Think of it as reduce with XOR and reduce with AND over a byte.
tt_um_wokwi_408216451206371329.try: Set In_0 to 1 and Out_0 lights at once, set In_1 to 1 as well and Out_0 goes dark (two is even), then set all eight inputs to 1 and Out_1 lights while Out_0 stays off.

tt_um_wokwi_408231820749720577.how: A combination lock with no memory. OUT1 to OUT7 just copy the first seven switches, like an LED bar showing what you have dialled. OUT8, the unlock line that would drive the servo, is a comparator that is 1 only when the eight switches spell the binary number 118. Despite the description there is no sequence tracking, only the switch positions right now.
tt_um_wokwi_408231820749720577.try: Set IN2, IN3, IN5, IN6 and IN7 to 1 and the rest to 0: OUT8 lights at once to unlock, and changing any single switch turns it off again.

tt_um_wokwi_408237988946759681.how: The description promises a counter to 99 on a two-digit display, but the gates that were actually manufactured contain no flip-flops at all. The chip is four inverters and some buffers: LED0, LED1, SEG_A and SEG_B are the inverted CLK, RST, BTN0 and a fourth unused input, SEG_C to SEG_F copy four unused inputs, and SEG_G, DIG1 and DIG2 are tied to 0. Most likely the Wokwi drawing was not wired to the output pins as intended, which is exactly the kind of thing Decap's proof exposes.
tt_um_wokwi_408237988946759681.try: Set BTN0 to 1 and SEG_A goes dark at once, set CLK to 1 and LED0 goes dark, and notice that Step and Run change nothing because there is no memory (SEG_B stays lit since its input is not on the bar).

tt_um_yuri_panchul_adder_with_flow_contr.how: An adder wrapped in valid and ready handshakes, like a producer and consumer talking through queues. Each 4-bit input and the 5-bit sum pass through a small 2-entry FIFO. When both input FIFOs hold a number and the output FIFO has room, the chip pops one from each, adds them and pushes the sum. If the consumer keeps sum_rdy at 0, the queues fill up and a_rdy and b_rdy drop to 0 to tell the senders to wait, which is called backpressure.
tt_um_yuri_panchul_adder_with_flow_contr.try: Press Reset, set a_data to 9, b_data to 8, a_vld and b_vld to 1 and leave sum_rdy at 0, then Step: after two steps sum_vld lights with sum_data 17, and after four steps a_rdy and b_rdy drop to 0 because every queue is full.
